utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second, please. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to deal with additional witness exhibit notification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, during the examination yesterday and the questions from the Trial Chamber, from the Bench, we have decided to use 1D553. It's a statement of the government dated 11 March 1998. It was brought up -- I think it was admitted with Professor Ratko Markovic, as my friend Tom Hannis used it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the only one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the only one -- well, all three are concerning Jashari incident. One is from the -- the first one, 1D551 is from the 5th and the second one is from the 6th and is 1D553 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will this witness be casting a different light on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would assume that the witness should answer the question about his knowledge and the knowledge of the president about the 11th of March statement of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you think he can add anything, that's fine. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I certainly hope. I mean, it came out yesterday so I couldn't proof him on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bear in mind you don't have to ask every witness about everything, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, but I feel much more comfortable if I -- I have only three witnesses so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Stamp, is there any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall allow you to do that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please bring the witness in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Zecevic will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to the evidence today. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kojic. How are you? Mr. Kojic, in the course of yesterday we talked about paragraph 18 of your statement in connection with the letter Minister Stojiljkovic never answered. It concerns the Jashari incident which occurred when Adem Jashari was arrested [as interpreted]. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, do you remember whether about a week later the Government of Serbia issued a communique, an official communique, about this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember it all that well. I couldn't really say. I think there was something, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at 1D553.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this was done in our office. Where it says A through A in handwriting, that's probably President Milutinovic's handwriting, and the number which you can't see right now, there's a number 458 on the document. That looks like my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this document was typed out in your office because it's headed "Republic of Serbia Ministry of Information"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it seems to be according to its form. I don't remember this text. I don't remember any of us typing it out. It's possible, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't remember either the text itself or the content?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, which part looks like your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number 458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you think is probably Mr. Milutinovic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A through A, A slash A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you show me what you're describing as A slash A by marking it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has a Serbian version. On the English version there is no translation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you can appreciate why --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got it. It's been marked on my Serbian version, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you need us to have the IC number of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one correction in the transcript, page 3, line 6, I said that during -- incident which occurred when Adem Jashari -- when attempt to arrest Adem Jashari was performed because, as we all know, Mr. Jashari has been killed during that attempt.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just a correction, Your Honours, that would be IC137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, yesterday we left off with your work on the documentation and the conversations which Professor Markovic and Kutlesic had with Chris Hill and Jim O'Brien. You said that there was a lot of that. Do you remember the exact volume and the time-period in which this took place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place between April 1998 up until -- towards the end of the year 1998. There were many versions - and when I say "many," I'm referring to suggestions put forward by one side and the other - which were then harmonized, translated. So I can explain what the procedure was, how this was done. The first proposal, as far as I know, came from the Americans, then it had to be translated, then comments were made on it, new words were inserted, new paragraphs in bold, or rather, what was unacceptable for our side was struck out. Later on, an edited text was produced which was supposed to look like definitive text. Then that had to be translated so that there were three or four versions of each proposal and then there were talks about it, negotiations when Hill and O'Brien came, new versions were produced and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to move a little closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, could you come a little closer to the microphone. You've got quite a soft voice and it's difficult for the interpreters to hear everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, in paragraph 37 you said that in the course of 1998 you typed out invitations and sent invitations for meetings or talks on behalf of President Milutinovic to Albanian leaders, but they did not reply except for one instance when Mr. Demaqi did reply. Do you know who Mr. Adem Demaqi was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. It was well-known. He was the political representative of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, could you please take a look at 1D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could 1D62 be put on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, when you spoke about those paper covers, is this the document we see now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see it in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There are some boxes here, sent by, received, subject, remark. The handwriting we see on the first page, whose is it, if you can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt it's the president's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please -- you can, of course, read the president's handwriting. Can you tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Here put the final copies, the end copies." And it's initialled by the president, who then said or instructed that this should be placed in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. This is the -- a letter for Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian text lower, please, I want to see the signature. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, when he signed letters going out of his office, did President Milutinovic use his initials, as here, or his full first and last name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he signed his full name, first and last name, and he put initials on copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the next page, page number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, this is a letter sent to Mr. Ljuan Koka, and you see it's dated the 14th of November, whereas at the end it says: "The meeting will be held in Pristina at 1100 hours on Wednesday, the 11th of November, 1998." Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, evidently more than one version was drawn up and different dates were used and this might have been done in error. A version might have been left where the date was not corrected. There must be the original of this letter, the original file in Word format in the president's office because all the letters sent out were kept in Word so that any error made when drafting the letters would have been corrected. The final version would certainly have had to be correct. It certainly didn't go out like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The mail -- the outgoing mail sent by the president, was it checked before being put into envelopes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was checked more than once. If any error was spotted, it would be corrected and then submitted again for the president's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any objections or complaints from anyone saying they had received a letter with a wrong date in it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, were the copies checked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was checked. If the original was in order, the copy would have to be in order too. But here in this case, evidently there must have been more than one version of this letter, probably containing different dates and different -- with a different content.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say in Word format, you mean the electronic versions. That's how the official copies of the letters that were sent out were saved. You mean on a drive somewhere in the president's office. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I wrongly understood that this was actually being put manually in a folder?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's correct, Your Honour. But they had a back-up system which was electronic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that, but in spite of checking the copies, we have one put away in the archives that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, if you look at this document, after this there are six other letters which are identical in content but addressed to other persons and they all have the identical mistake. They're dated the 14th of November and the meeting is allegedly scheduled to take place on the 11th of November. When these copies that we see here, if we put them in the context of the comment on the cover that you read out, do you think there is some connection or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, otherwise there would be nothing there. But as long as it says "keep the final versions or copies," this means that there were various versions and that probably by mistake the wrong version was kept in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kojic, a few moments ago we were discussing the documents that were actually the American proposal, Chris Hill's and Jim O'Brien's documents. Could you please open tab 15, that is 1D612, the date is the 14th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have the first page on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, in paragraph 49 -- no, sorry about that. 60, 60 is the number. I do apologise. Paragraph 60 where you refer to this document, you confirmed that you're the person who typed that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, probably. I cannot say for sure whether I did each and every document, but it looks as if I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the upper right-hand corner and tell me what that means.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the document was made after one of the meetings, or rather, one of the talks with Chris Hill and Mr. O'Brien.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this means, "SAD."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that that is the US proposal which -- which contains changes -- where all changes were inserted, that is, all the changes that we had proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you what the abbreviation "SAD" means.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United States of America, "Sjedinjene Americke Drzave," and this was on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So those are the documents. You have them in your file, don't you, are those the documents that you talked about from April until the end of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at tab 7, that is 1D712. This is a press release dated the 13th of May, 1998, concerning a delegation that was received from the MUP. You said there that traditionally on the occasion of the 13th of May such functions took place and the Ministry of the Interior would give you the entire text of the press release and all the other documents. Could you just explain to us what this actually did look like in practice, if I can put it that way. What is it that you received and what would you do with the documents that you would receive?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the programme of the celebrations would be sent, the participants involved, the press release, or rather, the draft press release. We would type out again the press release. If the president would have any objections, then that would be included, but I don't remember any. They would be received. The protocol would be informed. It's mainly the protocol people who dealt with them, receiving them and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you about the documents. So you'd get a document, or rather, a set of documents from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then what would you do with those documents or that document? You'd retype them on the Presidency memorandum, or rather, the memorandum of the president of the republic, or rather, on his writing-paper?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it would only be the programme of the celebrations, probably the participants, too, who would be received, that is, and the press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, when you received laws from the National Assembly that the president was supposed to promulgate through his ordinance, could you tell me what this looked like from a technical point of view?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received these laws from the secretary of the National Assembly. We would retype the text of the ordinance that was relatively short on the writing-paper of the president of the republic. That was done in three copies. Two originals would be typed out and one copy. So once the president signed this, one original would stay in the Presidency, in the president's office; the rest was returned to the secretary of the National Assembly so that it could be published further in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understood you correctly, as for the text of the ordinance, you would receive that from the National Assembly, too, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Not a single word was ever changed. We would only add perhaps the date and the number of the ordinance, because ordinances in the Presidency were kept chronologically, numbers 1 and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, just one question. Yesterday when we were talking about the mail that was coming in, would some mail ever arrive, a letter, a document that did not really belong to the area of work of the president? What would you do with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, of course, a lot of letters arrived, mail, that we would then forward either to the institutions in charge or that we would return to the documentation office so that it would be sent back to the person who sent the mail and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you would forward that to those who were, in your opinion, in charge of that, a ministry or something like that, you would send a cover letter, too, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to letters, please, tab 37, 1D624. These are the draft letters sent to some of the representatives of ethnic communities in Kosovo. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know those names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, the interpreters are still having difficulty hearing you clearly, so if you could speak a little louder it would help us greatly. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I'll do my best in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, once these letters were typed out, signed by the president, put in an envelope, how were they sent to the addressees, Mr. Rugova and the others? Do you know how this went?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 82 you said that the mail did not function, in Article 82 of your statement you said that the mail did not function and that sometimes you would give this to someone from the government who would go down there to Kosovo and Metohija, very often it was Mr. Andjelkovic, and you would send these letters to him so that he would have them delivered down there, taken to certain addresses through his associates. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Sending letters through normal mail to Pristina, to these addresses, that was out of the question, in view of the content of the letter, the person the letter was being sent to, in view of the fact that this was being sent from the office, there had to be a more reliable form of delivery through someone from the temporary Executive Council or something like that. I don't know. I cannot always remember specifically who the person was, and I did not really have to take care of that, who would actually have this delivered to a particular address.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But it was certainly important that the addressees receive these letters on time so that they could respond to invitations, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There would always be someone who would take that, as you mentioned. For the most part, it was Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you moving from that letter now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you leaving that exhibit now, moving on from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I do. Mr. Kojic, does the Serb copy have the date 20 November as the date of the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you go to the second paragraph of the letter and would you read the last sentence of the second -- that's the large paragraph. Just the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A result of that is the joint proposal of a framework agreement on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija which was published as a supplement on the 22nd of November in the Politika daily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please. Microphone, please. His microphone is off throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, can you give us any comment regarding the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I see that these copies have not been initialled, so I cannot say with certainty that these are the definite ones. Obviously, if this is the 20th of November, then here it cannot be the 22nd of November. This is either a technical error or there were other versions of these letters, too, that bear a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, a few moments ago you said to us that all letters before they are sent out were checked, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I don't see the president's initials here, and this leads me to think that this may be one of the versions that was not the final version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if the president did not initial this, that is not the final version?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it's supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about 1D62, we talked about 1D62 a while ago. This document was initialled by the president.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The error was probably uncovered only after the document had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about receiving documents from the National Assembly or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and simply pasting the document on to the president's memorandum. Can you please now look at tab 38, this is 1D722. This is an ordinance on promotions to the rank of second lieutenant of the police. 1D722, please, if that can be brought up, page 1. This is paragraph 83 of your statement. You see the ordinance, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the document you spoke about in terms of receiving a text in its entirety and merely typing it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we can have the whole -- minimise the Serbian version so we can see the whole page. I'm sorry. There is -- on the very top is -- yes. On the very top is the memorandum of the president. That is what interests me. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, at the top of that document it reads: "The Republic of Serbia, president," this is the memorandum that we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 3 of this document is signed, right, signed by Mr. Milutinovic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you go to page 4, please, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what this means, what we see on page 4.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the text that arrived from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. We made a copy, we typed it up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: From the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is the document that contained the ordinance on the next page, right, which you later pasted on to the president's memorandum and then the president signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the established practice?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kojic, Mr. Kojic, a question. Did President Milutinovic ever attend sessions of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, the cabinet for the Republic of Serbia; and if so, can you remember when specifically?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. Perhaps once, no more than once, but it's really difficult to remember exactly when and for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember him going in October 1998 to inform the cabinet on the agreement reached between Mr. Milosevic and Peter [as interpreted] Holbrooke, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did any notes ever reach the Presidency on the course of these sessions of the cabinet and what exactly transpired at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone ever getting in touch with Prime Minister Marjanovic to announce the arrival of the president to attend a cabinet session?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm entirely unaware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little; we can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please approach the microphone, sir, and speak up a little. Can you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the president receiving any invitations to attend any cabinet sessions; I think I can even go as far as to say he certainly received none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You never called the prime minister to announce the president's arrival, did you, nor did anyone from the cabinet call the prime minister to announce the president's arrival to attend a cabinet session?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm entirely unaware of anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the president ever went to a cabinet session, he would have had to inform someone, right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the protocol should know, the security should know. We certainly would have known but I'm entirely unaware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I finish maybe I should offer now the -- his statement and exhibits for -- to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it all of these exhibits are referred to in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to be issuing some guidance on dealing with exhibits in statements in future because this has caused certain technical problems which we must overcome, but you'll receive some guidance on that in the next few days. It doesn't apply in your case. We're just simply trying to improve the presentation for future cases, having learned of the difficulties that this can create. We're grateful for the efforts that are being made to deal with exhibits in writing, but there may be certain nuances and technicalities overlooked as a result of that, and we have to deal with ensuring that that doesn't cause difficulties at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see no objection taken to the statement or to the admission of any exhibits that had not already been exhibited and which are referred to in your statement. I also see no Defence counsel wishing to cross-examine, so it is over to you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kojic. Where were the presidential archives kept, in the office of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the president, or rather, in the office in which I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while you were there, who had responsibility to maintain and keep correct documents or copied documents in the archives?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us employed there had the same degree of access to the archives, had the same entitlement to use the documents, and the same responsibility to file them. There was no particular person who was specifically in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you will agree with me that it's a responsibility of high importance to ensure that correct copies of documents relating to the business of the Presidency are archived, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember a meeting of the 2 -- sorry, of the 12th of November, 2001, in the Presidency with the president and investigators from this office, that is, the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which year, November which year?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You remember that a party of lawyers and investigators, including one Mr. Milbert Shin and Mr. Kevin Curtis attended that day and interviewed President Milutinovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that they came twice, possibly three times, but I don't remember the date or the names. I think that the first time President Milutinovic spoke to anyone from the Tribunal it was Mr. Geoffrey Nice who was there with an associate. Later on, there were other persons whose names I can't quite remember or the dates they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Were you present in the office with President Milutinovic when he was interviewed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was present for part of the interview, but certainly not the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "the first one," do you mean the one with Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, were you present at the interview - and this is not the first one - where President Milutinovic spoke about the -- his efforts to speak with members of the Ministry of Interior in respect to the Jashari incident?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't think so. I can say I was trying to be handy. In case anyone needed a particular document, I would nip over to the archives and try to fetch it for them. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me remind you of something the record indicates that Mr. Milutinovic said and you could tell us if you remember him saying that. Mr. Milutinovic said in respect to this Jashari event that he called some officials, including the minister of the interior to brief him on it and that the minister did so brief him on it. Did you hear Mr. Milutinovic say that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I spoke earlier about the fact that I had informed Mr. Milutinovic about the event and I'm aware of the letter that he wrote and the reaction that he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would not be saying to us that Mr. Milutinovic would be lying or not speaking the truth when he told the OTP investigators that he spoke with the minister, would you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard that Milutinovic ever nor was I listening carefully to what he was talking about to the investigators nor do I remember as we speak, but I quite definitely don't remember anything that was worded in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Milutinovic said further on when asked about this interview with Minister Stojiljkovic he said: "But when you asked me about the subject of essential police work, they never discussed with me except, as I said to you, on 5th of March, 1998, and I called them here to ask them what really happened in the two villages in 1998." The president seems to be saying that he spoke to the minister at his office. Do you know of or recall whether or not President Milutinovic received the minister of interior at his office in respect to the Jashari incident in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. The log of the president's meetings - and this is probably a document in the possession of the ICTY - one should be able to check whether the meeting was held or not. As far as I remember, for quite long time after that Minister Stojiljkovic did not turn up at the president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For quite a long time after that Minister Stojiljkovic did not turn up at the president's office, for quite a long time after what?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the letter that the president sent to Minister Stojiljkovic seeking clarification about what had occurred at the Jashari -- this was sent sometime in the first half of March, possibly mid-March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Prior to that, was the minister a regular visitor to the president's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He only came very rarely; however, from that event on, at least a month had elapsed before Minister Stojiljkovic again showed up at the president's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you seem to think that that was an unusually long gap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given the president's request to receive a reply to that letter or maybe to receive a phone call about that, yes, I do think that that was an unusually long gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And after that visit, did he continue to visit the president from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say with any degree of certainty. His visits were rare, very rare, but the official log exists and this should be easy enough to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the occasion about a month after the Jashari incident when he did visit, what was the subject or purpose for his visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I don't even know whether it was a month. I should need to go back to the documents about the meetings. I didn't know the purpose of the visit at the time, but this was not the only visit where I was unaware of its purpose. I really hardly ever knew what they were likely to be discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Presumably -- if we may move on. Presumably the office of the Presidency, including yourself kept a record of the president's meetings as well as the agenda for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Record was kept of the meetings but not of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When the president went away from the office to official meetings, would you know who he was going to meet and what the meetings were about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the president hardly ever went to any meetings outside the Presidency building. The only exception to this were the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. He hardly ever went to the Assembly. I remember clearly that he went to the Assembly to discuss the Rambouillet talks. Maybe there was another occasion or two that he went. I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- I'm sorry. Please excuse me. If you could just get back to what I was asking about. I asked that because sometimes, you know, it's my experience sometimes when I had a secretary and I went away on business, she would know who was going to meet and what it was about. Now, would your office know where the president was going, who he was going to meet, and what the meetings would be about when he went to meetings away from the office?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out, the president did not hold any official meetings outside the Presidency building, aside from the exceptions that I have named. He went to the Supreme Defence Council meetings to see the president of Yugoslavia and to the Assembly, but I personally was not aware of any other meetings, official meetings, that he may have had outside the Presidency building. As for agendas or the purpose of any of these visits, now this was not something that we wondered about, except in situations where the purpose was generally known. For example, the visit to the Assembly was about Rambouillet. We knew that. Whenever he went to the Supreme Defence Council, we would as a rule know nothing at all about the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. There is evidence of meetings that he attended, apart from those that you have mentioned, which I would like to ask you about. And I just want to know if you knew about these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He -- Mr. Sainovic -- well, before I move on, I should probably, before I move on from Mr. Milutinovic, I was reminded that maybe I should mention for the record that the passages I referred to from Mr. Milutinovic's statement which is Exhibit 604 are from page 54, page 100, and page 180. I just do this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic in his interview with the OTP, and that's P605, he said that on many occasions in 1998 that he went to Kosovo, to Pristina to take care of matters involving the affairs there, he would return and report back and consult with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Milutinovic, and this is at page -- e-court pages 83 to 87 of his interview. Do you know about these consultations with Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic in 1998 in respect to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've been trying to point out so far, the president dealt with a number of different persons without ever informing us what precisely they were talking about, what precisely he was talking about to those persons. No minutes were kept of these meetings, nor did any of us attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you would not know about all the meetings that Mr. Milutinovic attended and what was discussed at that meeting -- at these meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my conviction that I was aware of all the meetings that President Milutinovic had. There were the regular meetings, but you also mentioned the times he travelled to Pristina. I think during the air-strikes he also travelled to Novi Sad and there may have been another one or two visits. I'm not sure I should class them as meetings. But that would be about it as far as any meetings he had outside the Presidency are concerned. All the other meetings were held in his office, and I can say that I had access to the documents that were based on these meetings and the same applied to all of the people I work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, I really don't propose to be here with this all day. Can you just focus on what I'm asking and answer as directly as you can. The consultations with Mr. Milutinovic and with Mr. Sainovic in respect to matters concerning Kosovo that Mr. Milutinovic -- sorry, the consultations with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Sainovic involving Kosovo that Mr. Milutinovic partook in, did you know or did you not know about these?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic at e-court page 197 to 198 also spoke of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you leaving this matter now of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He also spoke of another meeting which was attended by representatives of the military, the police, held at Mr. Milosevic's office in Belgrade in May 1998, which was presided over by Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milutinovic was there, and the parties received reports and discussed various matters in relation to the security situation in Kosovo. Did you know or did you not know of Mr. Milutinovic attending this meeting, this particular one, in May 1998 with those senior members of the army and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have any significant periods of absence or illness in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but I don't think so. I may have been absent for a few days at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself to be familiar, intimately familiar, with the work of your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic visit your office to see Mr. Milutinovic on occasions in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Mr. Sainovic did come in, did come to see Mr. Milutinovic a few times, but I really cannot recall any particular dates. What I do remember is that he certainly came to see him during the preparations for going to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milutinovic on occasions leave the office to go to visit Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, but I'm not aware of it. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it from what you're saying that Mr. Milutinovic regularly left the office without telling you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milutinovic had a routine, which I described in my statement. He would arrive at around 11.00, at around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've seen your statement. I wonder if you would just answer my question. Did he regularly leave the office without telling you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how to answer that question. He regularly left the office if he had a meeting -- well, if he had a meeting, he would tell us where he was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you not answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I don't know of any meeting he went to without telling us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're not likely to know about any meeting he went to without telling you. What I want to know is whether he left the office on occasions without telling you where he was going in the course of an ordinary business day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could turn briefly to 1999 and let me ask you this: Were you away from the office for any extended period for any reason in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to days or a special time of day?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Days.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember being away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you about one more meeting, and I refer to what Mr. Lukic said in his interview with the OTP, and that's P948 at page 137 to 138. He said that in May 1999 - and this is during the hostilities - he attended a meeting at a presidential villa in Belgrade. And among those present at the meeting were Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Ojdanic, Mr. Pavkovic, and the purpose of the meeting was to review the situation and to make note of the overview of the situation since the NATO bombing. And Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Lukic himself, Mr. Ojdanic, and Minister Stojiljkovic gave reports regarding the situation. This is May 1999. Do you know of Mr. Milutinovic attending that meeting? I take it you would agree with me that that would be a pretty important meeting. Did you know about this one?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that that meeting was held, nor do I know whether President Milutinovic attended the meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know if President Milutinovic during that period, that's the period of the bombing, attended any meeting at all where he was briefed by senior military or police personnel in respect to what was happening in the country? Forget about the date that I just spoke to you about in Mr. Lukic's statement. Just generally during the period of the bombing, do you recall if he attended any meeting where he was briefed by senior members of the military or the police in respect to what was happening in the country?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in the Presidency, but outside the Presidency I'm really not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milutinovic typically work on Saturdays?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not typically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke -- if we could move on, sir. You spoke in tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do move on, Mr. Stamp, you referred to part of Mr. Sainovic's interview which you said was on e-court pages 83 to 87. That was an accurate reference, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the -- and that's pages 1 -- sorry. 46 to 50 of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the area or the page that more directly addresses what I was saying is page 87 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that page 50 of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would respectfully advise the Court not to be too much troubled by the numbers at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I can't find the reference that you -- the quotation you gave about coming back and reporting or discussing matters with Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Milosevic, and I would like to see it in Mr. Sainovic's statement and I can't find it in these pages, I'm missing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have the extract here and I could find the pages and give them to the Court because this is something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me see the extract then, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just have a summary. The sense of what I said is contained in pages 83 to 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't get that sense from the four pages I'm reading at the moment, but obviously not as carefully as I would like to read them. However, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I will clarify that carefully later on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 to 16 of your statement you speak about Mr. Milutinovic -- about your office being aware of the -- or the call that Mr. Milutinovic received and that he made. I'm not quite certain about what this is intended to mean. Can I ask you something, could Mr. Milutinovic make direct phone calls without the office being involved in those calls, in making those calls?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all calls went through the secretary's desk, or rather, the telephone switchboard. And all the incoming calls were put through by the secretary. I'm not aware of any other kinds of calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he have a mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Of course he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he have a phone at his residence where you said he worked sometimes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what I'm trying to understand. Are you saying in these paragraphs, 13 to 16, that you would be aware of every single call that he received or that he made?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one has to take it with reservations because if he used his mobile phone, of course, we didn't know. But all official calls, all official incoming calls, went through the office, that is, through the secretary, both incoming and outcoming calls, in both directions. I can clarify. As regards the residence, even outside office hours, incoming calls came to the office. The secretary would make the connection with the residence and put the call through, and then either the president would answer or somebody else, whoever, and then the president was put on the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You say that you spoke with Vico Simonovic, and this is in paragraph 36 of your statement, in respect to the education agreement and Mr. Simonovic said --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is misspelled, or rather, it's the wrong name, it's Ratomir Vico. Professor Simonovic is another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Correct. And that on the basis of what he told you, you drew -- you had the impression that they -- withdrawn. But you're saying that he told you it was -- the Albanians were frustrating the education agreement. That is what is in your statement. I would like to show you a document which was addressed to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could P2855 be put up -- I beg your pardon, P2885.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that in all fairness because the witness will not be able to see the whole of the document, maybe he should be provided with the whole document in hard copy so he can get acquainted with the document if my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, wants to cross-examine him on that. Because of the e-court, he can only see one page at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear what the question is because obviously Mr. Stamp is entitled to conduct this the way he considers it appropriate. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just look at the cover page there and tell us what that indicates.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter from Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia to the President of Serbia Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there is a problem. This document is a letter to Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia but on the English it's a letter to Gelbard. Your Honour, the point of the problem is that this document which was given to us by the Office of the Prosecutor that they intend to rely on consists of three different documents, two in Serbian, originals, and one letter from Mr. Vincenzo Paglia. This is the document which we received from the OTP, and that is why I think it should be only fair that it has been given to the witness to comment on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the document you're relying on, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document is a letter in English which was sent to the president, Mr. Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia in respect to the education agreement, it's dated the 4th of June, 1998. It is written in English but the president's cover sleeve is, of course, in Serbian and there are two documents attached to it which are in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on, I'm not following this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. Now, Riaz, can you help us with why letter to Gelbard has come up in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The dates are also different, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with your English translation of the document that you want to rely on because it has a different date and bears to be a letter by S. Gelbard to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in particular President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That translation clearly is erroneous. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Let's just go on with it -- we can manage without the English. The witness has the B/C/S version and I think -- I see no objection to you continuing to cross-examine him the way you intended now that we're clear about what's missing and what you require to rectify. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to the version that you have, can you just tell us what the front page indicates, that is a cover page in the Cyrillic document you have there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have the documents. I have only the cover where it says a letter from Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia to the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could you look at page 3 of that document. What is that page indicating to you firstly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter which arrived on the president's instructions was sent to Mr. Ratomir Vico, who was in charge of those talks on education with the Albanian side and where Monsignor Vincenzo Paglia was involved as a mediator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate to the Court that that part of the exhibit, pages 3 and also page 4, another letter forwarding the monsignor's letter, are correctly translated in English in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So let's get back to the letter of Monsignor Paglia on page 2 sent to the president, and it's in English. Do you recall this letter going to the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it starts by saying, and I won't go through it, that the talks -- or I should start: "Mr. President. "The talks I had yesterday June 3rd in Belgrade were absolutely devoid of any result because of the Serb prejudicial position, which opposes the concession of spaces to the Albanian students in the faculties inside the central campus of the University of Pristina ..." So you would agree with me that the mediators in respect to the accomplishment or the purposes of the education agreement had completely or had a different view to the one which you told us in your statement that Mr. Vico expressed to you. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is completely unknown how would this witness know and can comment on this, what my learned friend is asking. We have seen from the page 3 that the document has been sent to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Stamp, what is the paragraph in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph is paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36, the witness is just stating what late Mr. Vico told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And -- and Mr. Stamp is perfectly entitled to cross-examine on whether he knows more than that on relation to this matter and know certain other facts which may be contained in this letter. So that objection is repelled. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall the question, Mr. Kojic? I could put it even more --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you right away that this document and most of the others I never delved into the contents except if I was personally curious, but I never went into the contents of particular documents because it was my job to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, you've been asked a different question from the one that you're trying to answer. You're being asked whether what's said in that letter is different from what you were told. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify the part of my statement that has to do with my conversation with Mr. Vico. That conversation took place sometime in 2002 or 2003 when we met in the street. We ran into one another in the street, and as we lived in the same neighbourhood - our homes are very close - we ran into each other in the street and talked of various matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need the whole history of your meeting with Mr. Vico. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has been added to our knowledge, Mr. Stamp, is that the reference in paragraph 36 is to events in 2002 or 2003, which is four or five years after the letter. And let's face it, what the witness says in his statement and what the letter says speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. I could move on, but perhaps I missed it, Your Honours. I -- I'm trying to find where paragraph 36 -- where it's indicated that paragraph 36 is 2002 to 2003 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's not, it's in the answer he's just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you will need to find out now from the witness, if you wish, what period in time Mr. Vico was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Vico told you about the situation in respect to the education agreement, do you know what period of time he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I asked him, Mr. Vico, how come so much time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the agreement was reached; that is to say sometime around 1996, 1997, 1998. I asked how come talks were held for so long and no agreement was reached. And his answer was that always some excuse was found in order not to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- I would move on from there. The evidence and the documents are self-explanatory. But I'm wondering if it is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is, indeed. Mr. Kojic, we have to -- Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my learned friend Mr. Stamp to avail himself of this opportunity, of this break, to show us where it is that Sainovic said what he had quoted just now. I cannot carry all the case files here with me and then when other people's witnesses refer to Sainovic, how can I have an easy reference? When a question is put in relation to Sainovic, could that please be put on the e-court or ELMO. We all make mistakes, not intentionally -- well, they that say God never makes mistakes, but then that remains to be seen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will try and clarify the situation in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be too late by the time you find the answer to that last point, Mr. Fila. The pages that were referred to do appear now that I read them again to be a proper basis for the question, and indeed you may well wish to have a look at them yourself during the break we're about to have because I may return to them. Mr. Kojic, we have to break now for half an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher; he will show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 11.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke in paragraphs 47 to 48 of your statement about the meeting at President Milutinovic's office with Mr. Rugova. Were you present in Mr. Milutinovic's office during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said, I believe, that Mr. Milutinovic normally flew, that is, took a plane, to Kosovo from Belgrade. Does that mean, I take it, that he could be in the office in the morning and could fly to a meeting in Belgrade [sic] in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said he also -- he normally returned -- he normally flew back the same day. He rarely spent the night in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more correct to say that he never spent the night in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At various paragraphs of your statement, particular paragraphs 18, 25, and 26, you refer -- or you speak about the work that the staff of the office would do to collate press reports, internet documents, a variety of things about matters that the president should be aware of and to brief the president. Did anyone in the office have a particular responsibility to ensure that the president was briefed about reports on important matters and events in Serbia and Kosovo in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a responsibility we all shared. Perhaps Olgica Vlahovic was a degree more responsible, but in her absence we did all the same work as if she were there. We would share the work. Somebody would watch CNN, somebody else would watch BBC, others would watch Sky News, yet others would look at the newspapers, we would make press clippings, but there wasn't a strict division. It depended on who worked in the morning, who worked in the afternoon. It's all the same work but it was distributed in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it in the period 1998 and certainly in 1999 up to June you would have paid particular attention to reports relating to events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you would have been aware of various international reports where there were allegations of crimes being committed by Serbian security forces against Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything that we considered noteworthy. It was obvious that there was a war over there. We put in into this review of major news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would look again at that question and answer the question you were actually asked, which is whether you were aware of international reports of allegations of crimes being committed by Serb security forces against Kosovo Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you say different international reports, what I understand that to mean is news agencies. Then what newspapers wrote, they were full of all sorts of correct and incorrect reports, exaggerated reports. We put more or less all of them on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean the answer to the question is yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say you put all of them on the list, you put all of them on the list of matters that you would brief the president about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at P2827. You see the president's cover page there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a letter by the deputy minister of information proposing that the Serbian state leadership address domestic and international public in connection with the accusations of crimes against Kosovo Albanians. If we could look at page 1 -- the next page of that exhibit. And while it is coming up, sir, could I just ask you was this one that Mr. Milutinovic would be shown personally, this letter from the deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we'll return to that. Since we're on the front page, it refers to reports in the western media and in the -- and I'm speaking about the first few lines in the body of the letter -- and in the Albanian press about the alleged massacre of Albanian civilians by the Serbian police in Gornje Obrinje. And if we look at the next page -- sorry, before we move to the next page could we just pause here. In the second paragraph, it refers to the possibility that the United Nations Security Council might become involved as a result of this -- of these news reports.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you or did the staff of the office, not necessarily you, make available to the president the various United Nations Security Council resolutions that were passed in respect to the events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I cannot assert anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to think about that. You had an intimate knowledge as to what the president was interested in and what the president should be apprised of. Wasn't the president interested in United Nations resolutions in respect to the events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, up to June?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is to be assumed that he was aware of those resolutions, that they had reached him, but now that you're asking me whether I can say with certainty, whether I can assert something like that, I do not remember that I personally prepared these resolutions for him and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say it is to be assumed that they had reached him, why would you working in the president's office and knowing the president assume that he would receive these resolutions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just -- well, probably because he was interested in the matter. It would be natural that these resolutions would reach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we leave this exhibit 2827 could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is some writing on the front page by hand. Can you say what that means?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Those are the initials of President Milutinovic, instructions set in the form of A through A that this should be archived. 11 is probably my own handwriting because this goes to binder number 11 on Kosovo and Metohija and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Do you recall the office receiving letters from the ICTY, from the Prosecutor of this Tribunal and --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I put P399 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this exhibit being shown to the witness, in fact, because it is not the whole exhibit. Actually, what happened is the following. Yeah, maybe the witness should be excused while we're talking about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't say that at the moment I understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You say -- the only question is whether he recalls receiving letters from the Prosecutor of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now he's being shown something which may jog his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, the document is not the complete document. That is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What if you only have part of the document. What's wrong with that? Tell me what the problem is about only showing part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The problem is that this document was never sent to President Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's another matter. What is the problem about prompting a person's recollection by showing him part of a document? Where is the problem in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the suggestion was that -- the question was does he remember that the document from the Prosecutor has been arrived. He said no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can deal with anything that arises from this in re-examination. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's P399.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a letter to the president of the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a question which perhaps, having regard to the statement made in the course of the objection, I'm not sure if it makes sense asking but I'll ask it nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not this letter was received by the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having ever seen this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not any letter from the ICTY was received by the president in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the president received a copy of the indictment in his office in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that we got the indictment off the internet or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sometimes we have to be careful. Somebody, I saw who and I heard who, answered the question before the witness answered it. And I just ask that we be careful. And answered it in the same terms as the witness later adopted it and I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean the reference to the internet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
