utterances.text: No, in the earlier part of what the witness said in -- just the answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness is wearing headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that doesn't excuse any counsel answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, by all means, Your Honour, I'm not saying -- I'm just referring to the witness's position when he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Stamp, you've got a much better answer than perhaps you anticipated if the witness had been one of the counsel in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it was not counsel who said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was further towards the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was right at the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In browsing the internet, did the staff at the Presidency concern itself with various reports that were published by NGOs, like Human Rights Watch, in respect to events that were occurring in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only if those reports came by way of headlines in some of the agency reports or newspaper reports, things like that. As for NGO reports in particular, I do not recall that we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any reports from Human Rights Watch or did you ever find any or did any ever come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not remember that. I do not remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P -- sorry, at 1D721. Perhaps -- and -- 1D721 first, next will be 1D705.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if my friend on the other side has copies in Serbian. Perhaps the witness could be handed copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe -- I'm sorry. If I may be of assistance, 1D721 is tab number 12, so the witness has it in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say what that is? Is it a list that was sent to the president?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that this was addressed to the office of the president, not to the president personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- it's a list of citizens killed in Kosovo and Metohija, and if you turn quickly to tab 47 you will see 1D705 -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, it's 1D707 I want. If you turn to tab 11, you'll see 1D707. I'm sorry it's not 705 we want to look at, it's 707. That's another list, and this is a list of civilians and MUP personnel abducted in Kosovo during the same period, January to July 1998. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was sent to the Presidency by the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how often these reports were sent? Were these sent twice a year or --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall these being monthly reports. They would simply do a survey up to such and such a date, but I don't think it was done on a regular basis, on a weekly or monthly basis or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who requested that these reports be sent to the Presidency from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I think these reports were distributed to several addresses in Yugoslavia. I don't think they were sent only to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive similar reports listing Albanian, Kosovar Albanians, who were casualties of activities by Serb forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these reports also contained figures on Albanian victims, maybe not this particular one, I haven't looked at it. But I think in general in these reports Albanian victims were reported as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not only asking you about Albanian victims. I was asking about Albanian victims of crimes committed by Serbian forces. Did you receive reports from the Ministry of Interior in respect to that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further to ask of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, you were asked about things that Mr. Sainovic had said in an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. And in summary, it was put to you that in 1998 Mr. Sainovic said that he was -- or he met frequently with President Milosevic and that Mr. Milutinovic attended these meetings. And while it's not entirely clear what period the following answer relates to, it could be May or -- May and June 1998 and it could be a bit later than that, but it's sometime in 1998. And in reference to these meetings he said: "This was the time when there was a lot of meetings, you know, held daily and I really couldn't tell you exactly because this wasn't one historic meeting." So he's being about one meeting and he can't remember the precise details. But he does say that these meetings with Milosevic at which Milutinovic was generally present were held daily over a period of time. Now, do you recollect a period in 1998 when Mr. Milutinovic regularly, on a daily basis, over a period of time went to the office of the president of the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if you would try a bit harder then, please. Just think very carefully about 1998 when there was trouble, for present purposes it might be said, instigated by the KLA and a considerable degree of tension within the republic. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember that. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a period in 1998 when Mr. Milutinovic regularly left the office to meet with Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm also unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.text: It's all been -- pending translation.

utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no other witnesses to call in our Defence case. There's one matter regarding exhibits, and I seek your guidance on this and I have a proposal to make. utterances.text: Your Honour, I find myself even busier now than I was in July and I would request that they file a bar table motion because I -- I simply don't know what the relevance is -- oftentimes I don't have any objection for authenticity for most of those documents but I don't know the relevance and it side-tracks me from other things I'm trying to focus on at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other matter I think can be dealt with just now. The Prosecution and Defence jointly responded on 16th August to an order for submissions on the joint Prosecution and Defence notice about translation of exhibits admitted into evidence by agreement. The Chamber accepts that proposal and orders that these documents shall be removed from the record of the proceedings pursuant to Rules 54 and 89. In paragraph 4 of the submission, the parties inform the Chamber of six other documents that are duplicates of exhibits already on the record. The Chamber hereby orders, again pursuant to Rules 54 and 89, that these duplicative documents shall be removed from the record of the proceedings. That leaves outstanding just the question of the constitutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have reached the agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor, and we will be filing it shortly. It just needs us to go out and undersign. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we order you then to file that by close of business on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it will be filed today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, our order is close of business on Friday and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be a suitable time also to intimate to you that we have been able to arrange to sit on this same schedule, that's till 3.30, on Monday of next week. Now, this is to try to accommodate the problems that have arisen with Mr. Fila. Next week's a week where I suspect other court time might come available because it's immediately following the recess. It's plain that we are not going to be able to sit these longer hours for any significant periods later in the trial, probably from next week. So it does make sense, in our view, to make use of that time when it is available, particularly because we asked you to ensure that you had witnesses here to fill any gaps that arose in the schedule and they've been here for some time. It may be that it's only Monday we can do this but we will wait and see if other possibilities arise. That takes us then to the case for the second accused, which you propose to open with a speech, Mr. Fila. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for all your efforts, Your Honour; otherwise, I would probably stand accused of invading Holland, given the number of witnesses that I have called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so far you have heard the position of the Defence in relation to the accused Sainovic in our preliminary motion alleging defects in the form of the indictment and in our pre-trial brief. To repeat this same thing all over again would be a boring exercise for me and for you alike. That is why I choose to merely state that I abide by all these positions and by all the positions that we, the Defence, stated in our 98 bis submissions. The Defence will today deal with what is peculiar to the position of Nikola Sainovic in the indictment, including his position and his role in the alleged joint criminal enterprise. In the reply by the OTP dated the 15th of August, 2002, to the preliminary motion by the Defence alleging defects in the form of the indictment, the OTP claim that no suggestion is made anywhere that Sainovic had de jure authority over persons who were the direct perpetrators of crimes, but rather that Sainovic's authority was de facto and that he should prepare to defend from allegations of de facto command responsibility. This was the position, although the wording of the indictment was amended many times, and this position was not given up in the last version of the indictment, saying that Sainovic on instructions from Slobodan Milosevic had de facto power over the accused. So far the Prosecution has not adduced a single shred of evidence to support this theory. Therefore, the Defence can only conclude that what the Prosecution probably had in mind was the Joint Command, since - and that at least is beyond dispute - Sainovic had no de jure command authority in Kosovo. The only thing that remains, therefore, is the Joint Command. If there is no Joint Command, then there is no responsibility. If there is no evidence to show that Nikola Sainovic was sent there by Slobodan Milosevic, then there can be no instructions issued by Slobodan Milosevic for the accused to act in compliance with. The accused will show through our witnesses that the Joint Command in the sense construed by the Prosecution and as understood by the Trial Chamber in its 98 bis ruling, never existed. It is the Defence's position that such a command never existed, not in 1998 or in 1999, not in the sense that one of its members or even its commander having been Nikola Sainovic. Witnesses such as Milomir Minic, Zoran Andjelkovic, and Dusan Matkovic will confirm that the meet the meetings held in 1998 in Pristina were not meetings of some Joint Command. They will also confirm that those meetings - whatever we choose to term them - stopped when the anti-terrorist operation ceased and certainly no later than late October 1998. Never again did these same persons meet again in Kosovo and Metohija. The Defence shall call witnesses to explain all the places that Nikola Sainovic went to throughout 1998 and 1999. Based on witness testimonies, it will become clear that throughout 1998 and after the end of the above-mentioned operation, Nikola Sainovic became the president of the committee for cooperation with the OSCE mission. He spent his days and his nights working with the mission at meetings. He travelled to Rambouillet and to Paris. He was involved in negotiations with Mr. Rugova. He spent time in Bor, his native town in eastern Serbia, on holiday, having completed his activities in relation to Rugova. So much moving about and so much involvement, as Mr. Cosic said the other day, can indicate only one thing: How absurd the conclusion is that someone who is supposed to be in command of a Joint Command in Kosovo and Metohija spent so much time outside Kosovo and Metohija. General Vasiljevic's statement shows that he never even hinted that Sainovic might have been the commander or a member of the Joint Command, which is the claim that is being made. Hence, the Defence accepts that Nikola Sainovic spent some time in Kosovo and Metohija throughout 1999 and 1998, but not as part of some Joint Command which purportedly existed in order to convey instructions by Slobodan Milosevic. Defence witnesses Momir Bulatovic, Zivadin Jovanovic, and Andrej Milosavljevic will prove that Mr. Sainovic was in Kosovo and Metohija on orders from the federal -- from the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of which he was president. Nikola Sainovic was in Kosovo in his official capacity as deputy prime minister and he was perfectly within his legal powers. As federal deputy prime minister in charge of international relations, Nikola Sainovic spent time in Kosovo and Metohija in order to meet with foreign diplomats and representatives present in Kosovo and Metohija as part of the KDOM, and later as part of the KVM. In order to be able to participate in talks with foreign diplomats and other representatives on an equal footing, he had to get information. The federal government had no powers over the republican police. He got the best information on what went on in Kosovo and Metohija in direct contact with representatives of the army, police, and civilian bodies in Kosovo, as well as in his contacts with foreign representatives. Therefore, the Defence claims and the Defence shall prove that Nikola Sainovic was in Kosovo and Metohija on orders from the federal government of the Republic of Yugoslavia as deputy prime minister in charge of international relations. Given the amount of different functions that he was exercising at the time - and this has been clearly shown so far - he certainly could not have formed part of any sort of Joint Command, even if such a thing had existed. One has to draw a distinction between the three periods that are relevant to this trial. The first period comprises the summer of 1998 and goes on until the completion of the anti-terrorist operation in the autumn of 1998. Throughout this time Mr. Sainovic is in Kosovo and Metohija on orders and having received approval from the federal government as deputy prime minister, who since 1996 had been in charge of international relations. He was appointed by its president, Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic. That is the first relevant period. The second relevant period is the period of the Kosovo Verification Mission. On account of his experience in working with foreign diplomats ever since the implementation of the Dayton Accords as well as his Kosovo experience, at the proposal of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia appoints Mr. Sainovic as president of the commission for cooperation with the OSCE mission. It was within this context that his many meetings with the representatives of the Kosovo Verification Mission took place, and they themselves gave evidence about this before this Trial Chamber. It will be demonstrated what the true nature of the mission was, what its tasks were, and what its powers were. It will be demonstrated how much effort was required for all these jobs to get done, which would have been simply too much for someone who purportedly was also in charge of commanding some kind of a Joint Command. And one should also not underestimate NATO. In the third period, the period of war, Nikola Sainovic, again having received orders from the federal government, gets involved in the process relating to Mr. Rugova and in negotiations with Mr. Rugova. After the departure of Mr. Rugova, Mr. Sainovic travels to his native Bor on holiday, which is to say the least slightly unusual for someone who is purportedly the commander of a Joint Command. He is now absent from his purported command post amid air-strikes. It is quite unusual that the commander of this Joint Command, as he is purported to be, in the thick of the action is simply absent dealing with the evacuation of hazardous chemicals in Baric near Belgrade. This person is an engineer by profession. He is federal deputy prime minister and has no military or police experience whatsoever, yet he's represented to be the commander of units that are being subjected to permanent air-strikes by NATO. The Defence will show that Nikola Sainovic, as federal deputy prime minister in charge of international relations, spent time in Kosovo, performed functions that he was sent there to perform as the honourable and conscientious man that he is. Mr. Sainovic implemented policies in the way described by Prosecution witnesses and that will be described by Defence witnesses, too, such Prosecution witnesses as Petritsch, Burns, Phillips, Kickert and others. Mr. Sainovic wanted peace not war; by virtue of that very fact, he can bear no personal responsibility for what happened in Kosovo and Metohija and cannot be responsible for the events alleged in the indictment. The Prosecution claims that Nikola Sainovic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution claims that there was such a thing as a joint criminal enterprise and that Mr. Sainovic was one of its members. The Defence claims that there was no such thing as a joint criminal enterprise in 1998 or, for that matter, in 1999 or, for that matter, during the Rambouillet talks or during the war itself. For a joint criminal enterprise to have existed and in order to be able to claim that Mr. Sainovic had a part to play in it, certain conditions must be met, objective as well as subjective. The objective conditions would be the existence, the existence of a common purpose, design, or intention to commit a crime from Articles 2 through 5 of the Statute of this Tribunal. It would be necessary for Mr. Sainovic to have committed an act that would have contributed to the commission of this joint criminal enterprise, design or intention. As for the subjective aspect, there are two possibilities in relation to Nikola Sainovic. The first possibility is that he committed these crimes that he's charged with deliberately as part of a plan. The other possibility is that these crimes exceeded the scope of the plan, and Mr. Sainovic could have foreseen that by his acts he would contribute to the commission of crimes. In order for this other modality to be accepted, one must first establish that he had foreseen the possibility of exceeding the scope of a purportedly pre-existing plan. Mr. Sainovic should be conscious of the fact that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise that might cause certain actions that were initially not covered by his original intention. So far the Defence has not seen any of these elements actually proven in this trial, no objective elements and no subjective elements. The Defence will show that Mr. Sainovic acted in his capacity as the federal deputy prime minister and in compliance with decisions made by that government. That government was not set up in order to commit a joint criminal enterprise. If indeed he happened to be somewhere where certain words were spoken, spoken perhaps by a high-ranking state official, perhaps even the highest-ranking state official, words that might indicate the commission of a crime, presence itself is not sufficient to lead us to conclude that Nikola Sainovic was a member of some joint criminal enterprise, nor indeed that such an enterprise existed. What one should establish is his active participation in the commission of this crime. Finally, let me conclude this. Nikola Sainovic was a national delegate and a member of the federal parliament. He was appointed federal deputy prime minister. He carried out the tasks which this government and its president entrusted him with, and these tasks were to push for a peaceful solution of the problems in Kosovo and Metohija and to strive for equality between all nations and national minorities there. In one word, Nikola Sainovic was a man of peace, and this was clearly demonstrated by evidence given by OTP witnesses. It will be demonstrated yet again by our own Defence witnesses. Thank you very much, Your Honours. This completes my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Now, who is to be your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I made a system that will function from one witness to another. That's the way our system works. It's one and then the other, not like yours from here to there. The first witness is Mr. Momir Bulatovic, who was prime minister of the federal government on which Mr. Sainovic served as deputy prime minister. As you remember, I told you that you would have renowned people as witnesses, high-ranking persons as witnesses, and indeed those are the people I have called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he is the first witness, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] I call Mr. Bulatovic. Could he please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Are we to receive binders of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have done that already. They're right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be sensible then for us to break now, as long as all the preparations are complete and that we don't come back and find that there are other issues to be bandied about before we start listening to the witness. Now, have you completed any preliminaries associated with leading this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in one part I asked for an extension of 65 ter because after Mr. Markovic's testimony there is the question of the Supreme Defence Council that has to be dealt with, and he was twice a member and once he attended -- I mean Mr. Bulatovic. He was president of the Republic of Montenegro for a while. So could you please rule on that and I'm sure that the Prosecutor is not opposed to this in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I saw the request. I'm not opposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow you to examine the witness on the Supreme Defence Council. Anything else? Well, when we come back, no doubt there will be binders at our feet or on the table and we'll be ready to go straight into the evidence of the witness. We'll adjourn now and resume at the normal time of 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please bring Mr. Bulatovic into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document you will be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. I would like to make a special plea to you before we begin your evidence, and that is when a question is asked by Mr. Fila, would you pause before answering that question until you think the translation will have been completed into English; otherwise, it is very difficult for the interpreters to keep up with the two people speaking the same language. And Mr. Fila will do exactly the same when you answer him, he will pause before asking you the next question. And that way I assure you, although it sounds as if there might be delay, it's actually a way of speeding things up. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bulatovic, could you please give us your name and surname first and then let's get started.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what offices you held from 1992 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1992, I was elected president of the Republic of Montenegro. These were direct elections, democratic ones as assessed by the international community. I remained in that office until the beginning of 1998. And then in May, on the 20th of May, 1998, I was elected prime minister of the federal government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could other microphones please be switched off, there's a great deal of background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you made up your government and could you tell us who the persons on your government were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That question requires an additional explanation by your leave. There was the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was made up of the coalition partners from Montenegro and from Serbia. These were the democratic party of socialists as a socialist party from Montenegro and the socialist party of Serbia. And the Yugoslav left from the Republic of Serbia. Also there was a sufficient majority in this way to establish a government -- form a government. However, due to internal political differences, Montenegro -- the ruling, then-ruling party of the democratic party of socialists split into two. There was one -- there was a different majority that was set up in Montenegro that had a different political composition as compared to the federal parliament. Wishing to ensure continuity of these policies, the federal government was toppled. This federal government was headed by Prime Minister Dr. Radoje Kontic from Montenegro. In effect, he was chancellor of that government. Instead of him, I came from Montenegro because I got the mandate to form a government and support for that government. The programme of the government that I presented to parliament was -- won a two-thirds majority whereas a simple majority was required. I received the support of MPs from both republics in both chambers of parliament. This background is important because of the following. The change in federal government was effected in order to have continuity. That is why I as prime minister designate practically took over on the new government practically all the people who were there originally from the Republic of Serbia; that is to say, in the previous government as well. Changes did take place, not in order to change Yugoslav policy, but in order to respond to the changes that then started in the policy of Montenegro and that constituted a deviation from the policy pursued until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that mean that that is how you took over Nikola Sainovic as deputy prime minister inter alia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among others, I had the honour and pleasure of having Mr. Nikola Sainovic serve on my government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your view, did the federal government manage to develop all its capacities as envisaged by the FRY constitution from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, and that was a special problem. We focused on that, we focused our efforts on that. Actually, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came into being in 1992 as a consequence of the fact that the previous country, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia fell apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the first days when this state started functioning, it was subjected to sanctions by the international community, punishment by the international community. There was a war in the immediate neighbourhood, in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia. The leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia made great efforts by way of participating in international conferences to contribute to bringing this war to an end. Regrettably, all of this went on for very long and the war ended only through the peace accords in Dayton. In this process, and there is no denying that, the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia gave a decisive contribution. Many people at that time said that that was the crucial contribution. However, on account of that, we did not have enough time to develop our internal capacities. Inter alia, for example, the entire field of the security services which according to the constitution belonged to the Federation had not been set up at federal level. So the method of work during all those years was reflected in an intensified effort to coordinate the existing services and institutions and organs that existed at republican level and, on the other hand, those that existed at federal level. The federal state had great powers in the field of foreign policy, and that was not touched in the entire diplomatic and consular representation of the country was under our jurisdiction we also had customs as our own revenue. As for taxes, they were in the hands of the federal organs and on the other hand the two republics that were members of the Federation had their share of the taxes. At any rate, we ourselves were not satisfied with the level of functioning of this federal state. If we compare this to what the constitution envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's try to cut this short a bit, what was the authority of the federal government and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government was the sponsor of bills related to the budget. Defence was the major item in the budget. From that point of view, the federal government had a logistic support as people call it and it needed to ensure resources that were indispensable for the functioning of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you said that the security services had not been set up at federal level. What were you referring to by "the security services"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant exactly what I said. According to the federal constitution, the field of security was supposed to be dealt with at federal level as well. There were services that dealt with it at the level of the member republics and there was this one service that was a specialised one within our diplomatic service, that is to say attached to our embassies abroad. We never managed to bring together all of these services as envisaged by the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This special position of the federal state, did it cause a special way of functioning of the federal state?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Many attempts were made to resolve existing dilemmas on the basis of the functional principle. We did not have time to look at what particular powers had to be taken from some republican ministries and given to the federal ministries. It was much simpler at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We are not going to have all of this in the transcript and then there's no use in having this kind of discussion if it's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It is much easier to discuss this than to have the problem actually resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From that point of view, did you have some meetings of coordination with, say, the republican prime ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This was a regular practice that went on for years, especially while Zoran Lilic was head of state of federal -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Radoje Kontic prime minister. We met often because it was necessary to overcome the institutional inconsistencies that existed and we did not have time to wait for the processes of getting all of this coordinated in the federal parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999, did your government face a crisis in Kosovo-Metohija and did these problems come into being then, in 1998, or had they been there for much longer than that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my government faced this problem as one of the most difficult ones conceivable for resolving. With the permission of the honourable Trial Chamber, I would like to say that my first experience related to Kosovo and Metohija go back to the days of my boyhood. My father was a Partizan and he fought in the anti-fascist war against German and Italian units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, if I may interrupt you, this question is confined to 1998 and 1999. Many people come here who want to tell us the whole history of Kosovo throughout their lifetimes. We don't have time to deal with that. In fairness to everyone else who has been put in the same position, we would be grateful if you would confine your answer to the years referred to in the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Of course, I will abide by that. I asked you for your permission, but I have to say that it is part of one's background and one's train of thought, experience that one had and everything that one learned and heard but yes, I will abide by what you said. We had a serious problem to deal with and my entire government felt this to be organised and growing terrorist violent threats to the constitutional order in a part of the Republic of Serbia, in certain areas of Kosovo and Metohija. We acted like any other state would act in relation to the fact that at that time in Kosovo and Metohija what was sought was not dialogue. That is something that we and the Government of Serbia were all prepared to engage in dialogue but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again you're departing from the question. You've answered the first part of it, which is that you were faced with a crisis in 1998 and 1999. And you were then asked whether the problems came into being in 1998 or had they been there for much longer than that. Now, what's your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that the Special Envoy from the United States Robert Gelbard in February 1998 said that in his assessment the activity of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army was undoubtedly terrorist activity, and he said that the KLA was a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the problems started before you came to power?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was at the heart of the problem in Kosovo, the clash in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There are many facts and many statements and a lot of evidence showing that what was underlying was the wish to create a united state of Albanians in this area. Some people call it a greater Albania but at any rate it is the wish for all Albanians to live in one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know how what happened in the state of Albania in 1997 affected the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I know that very well because Albania is a neighbouring state and I, as president of Montenegro, visited my colleague Sali Berisha in 1993. That was the first visit that took place after 50 years of statesmen of the two countries. During communism there was a firm border. For 50 years the closest relatives and friends -- even the closest of relatives and friends could not get together. When I went to Albania we reached a satisfactory agreement as far as I'm concerned to soften the border, so to speak, so the relatives and friends could meet so that normal communication could start, although from a political point of view we disagreed on most issues. In 1997, for reasons that I cannot go into, there was a collapse of state structures in Albania. What was shocking to me was that all of a sudden a civilised, organised structure simply disappeared. The population attacked warehouses of the army and the police that did not exist and they took an enormous amount of weapons. Proof of this is that we in Montenegro and in Kosovo and in Serbia found these weapons and it was easy to recognise it because these weapons were Chinese made. Albania for a long period of time enjoyed Chinese support and their warehouses were full of these weapons. In this same period of time, which was very sad, an attack took place against all public structures in Albania; that is to say schools were destroyed, roofs were taken off hospitals, there was a lot of looting. I know that because thousands and thousands of trucks from Albania crossed the border into Montenegro and they were selling as scrap a lot of Albanian infrastructure, including the railroad that links our two states. There is something that is of interest to this case, and that is that enormous quantities of weapons went to Kosovo and Metohija. I saw that the BBC covered this and had documentary programmes dealing with this. I know that at that time a Kalashnikov would cost $20 and everybody wanted to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with prices, how --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you repeat that question, please, it was not heard by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you how arming was financed in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: According to all the knowledge I had as president of Montenegro and later as the prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a significant share in the financing was accounted for by the Albanian mafia that was widespread throughout Europe and that, in fact, forced Albanian economic emigres from Kosovo and Metohija to make regular payments into some kind of a budget and that is probably how most of this financing took place. This is what I found out as I carried out my duties on the basis of all the information that we received from our services. I had many opportunities to talk to representatives to foreign countries, especially the European mission, or rather, ambassadors of EU countries. I understood that they had similar information and that they shared the same kind of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did our government caution people about the channelling of such resources from western Europe in order to finance criminal and terrorist activity? Did our government warn against this and did our government ask for this to be stopped and to stop this kind of money from smuggling being brought into Kosovo and Metohija and used for buying weapons?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We did that systematically, but this was never reflected publicly. That is to say that in politics and in diplomacy there is always a higher goal on account of which it pays off to keep quiet about another truth. In private everyone agreed to us, but in public they always said, No, no, that's not the case, you're just using this as a pretext in order for you to carry out some kind of strange policy of your own in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you and other ministers of your government in your contacts with the collocutors in western Europe warn them of this, that is, that money was being collected and did they take any steps for this to be stopped?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We did this almost daily but to very little effect. I think that our colleagues from the big and developed countries had even better and more precise information than we did. They did not, however, see this as a problem which would require action on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic participate in this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In all his activities to do with Kosovo and Metohija in the government, Mr. Sainovic put forward political facts and advocated a political and diplomatic approach to the problem. These arguments were part of our overall approach to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have just heard that you held high offices, both in Montenegro and in the federal state did you participate in the Dayton talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Dayton as a member of the Yugoslav delegation headed by the then-president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic. The president of the Republic of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic and I as the president of Montenegro were members of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There's something constantly hanging in the air. Was there any mention of solving the Kosovo problem in Dayton? If anyone mentioned it, who did and what did they say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly, the negotiations in Dayton went on for more than 20 days. It was one of the most exhausting experiences all the participants had had. Of course in the corridors there was talk of Kosovo, but officially in all the talks from which the overall agreement on Bosnia and Herzegovina stemmed, there was no mention at all of Kosovo. It should be borne in mind that the Dayton Peace Accord did not solve just the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the so-called military annexes, it also established the principles of regional military stability. From the end of 1995 onwards, according to the same principle, the Army of the FRY, the Republic of Croatia, and that of Bosnia and Herzegovina developed in the same way. This was a process in accord with the Vienna Convention. One must bear in mind that the size of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1998 was agreed in Dayton, and it was raised to an internationally acceptable level through constant communications which we had through Vienna with Zagreb and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there was talk about Kosovo only in the corridors?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, you had some talks with members of the American administration in Washington in 1996. Will you tell us very briefly why you went to Washington, who you talked to there, and what was offered to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the most important thing in every politician's career is a visit to Washington. It's indubitably the centre of political, military, and economic power. I visited the USA as president of Montenegro on three occasions. This visit in 1996 was important for the following reason. In November of 1996, I had talks in the American congress with an eminent congressman Lee Hamilton who was the president of the Foreign Affairs Committee. He headed the lobbyists who advocated the position that our police and military forces were maltreated and persecuting the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. I repeat, this was in 1996 when there was not yet any major conflict, when there were no major incidents in Kosovo and Metohija yet. My position was different and I wanted to draw his attention to the fact that the Albanian majority which existed then in Kosovo was seriously threatening the rights of the minority there, Montenegrins and Serbs. However, Mr. Hamilton was lobbying for the rights of the Albanians. As I was unable to achieve any kind of agreement with his associates, then the truth that was my truth, that I had come there to deliver, was unable to get through the American congress. Lobbying is a part of American political life, but we did not have enough money to ensure the support of lobbyists to meet the support of such a large group. The second meeting I had which was most significant to me was in the White House. I spoke to the deputy secretary for national security, I think his name was Aleksandar Wirshbo [phoen] and the special advisor of then-President William Clinton, who's name escapes me for the moment. The main thrust of these talks was that there would be unrest in Kosovo, that America would send 50.000 of their soldiers to Kosovo and Metohija, as they had sent 50.000 to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that this was a reflection of their concern which had arisen because of the relations then existing in the world which had to do with misunderstandings between NATO and certain countries of the European Union. There was a lively discussion taking place at the time to the effect that the European Union had to strengthen its defence role and it could not do so unless it first reduced the role of NATO. I was then told that Slobodan Milosevic, who had publicly been proclaimed as the one to get the most credit for peace in Bosnia after the Dayton Accords would be blamed for the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija. I was offered to turn my coat and to join another group of people, those who deserve the support of the American bureaucracy and administration by distancing themselves from Serbia and its expected role in Kosovo and Metohija. I have too much knowledge and experience not to consider the iron rules of the strategy and policies of the great powers, but to my great regret the interests of these great powers were -- came into play precisely in the country of which I was a representative, they collided there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You also participated in many other international gatherings. In the regional gathering of presidents of states and prime ministers in 1998 in Antalya, what was said about Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That was the second meeting of heads of states or prime ministers of south-eastern Europe. The first one was attended by President Milosevic on behalf of the FRY, and the second in Antalya in Turkey was attended by our delegation headed by myself. At the same time, the Special Envoy Richard Holbrooke was in Belgrade and the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was being negotiated which I hope we will discuss later. What sticks in my mind is the fact that when I landed in Antalya in Turkey, instead of the scheduled meeting of heads of state, what was in the headlines in the most influential Turkish newspapers in Milliyet was NATO bombers and a big headline: "We will attack." All the participants of the gathering, which was devoted to regional stability, had been informed that NATO would attack Serbia and the FRY. Although there was no specific pretext at the time, but in all our talks everybody expected us to work some kind of miracle to avoid NATO air-strikes. The then-Turkish Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz in bilateral meeting we had did not know how to answer my question. 40.000 members of the Turkish minority were then living in Kosovo and Metohija and they were having no problems with the legal authorities of Serbia. They were not members of any terrorist groups. After the NATO air-strikes, not a single one could remain in the area, hardly a single one. My question was: How can you protect human rights even if they are threatened to a large extent by sending in bombers to conduct random air-strikes? Everybody spoke about the damage their countries would suffer because of their air-strikes, I mean from the neighbouring countries. What tourists would visit any neighbouring countries while there were air-strikes going on in Kosovo? However, we had no power, no ability, to stop the air-strikes. Everybody knew they were going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the situation, in your view, in Kosovo and Metohija in the spring and summer of 1998? How do you assess the situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My government considered this issue more than once. It was tabled before the parliament and before the public. The situation was very, very difficult. We knew that an armed rebellion cannot be stopped by military or other means alone. We persistently insisted on political dialogue and a political solution. I think the same happens everywhere in the world. I am deeply sorry that so many people have been killed, members of all ethnic groups, all nationalities. We could have accepted the outstretched hand for political dialogue which was being offered first and foremost by the Republic of Serbia and then also by the federal government. We could have prevented these dreadful consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did terrorist activities increase? How were they manifested in the spring of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, quite simply, demands were being made for a deblockade of particular roads and communications in Kosovo and Metohija and what was heard officially from the state organs, there was an escalation and there were more large-scale terrorist activities. And this required an appropriate response by our security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any murders? Abductions? And so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately there were murders, crimes, things that any reasonable person would find of deep concern and would want to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now look at -- you have a bundle of documents before you. Please open tab 1. The document bears the number 2D371. Mr. Bulatovic, don't read it out. We're all literate, we can all read for ourselves. Just comment briefly on what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is in my view a very significant stage in the search for a political solution and in trying to formulate a compromise with the international community. This is the result of the meeting between the president of the Russian Federation Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin and the president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic. The principles agreed on are absolutely acceptable and they represent a starting point. One of the starting points for the agreement reached with the OSCE by our government in setting up the verification mission. This is a very significant step but it is only one of the steps that led to the political and the state compromise that we as the Government of the FRY achieved with the OSCE monitoring mission, which is the broadest political organisation of the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As a result of this joint statement, did not several hundred foreign OSCE diplomats arrive within the scope of the first KDOM, the Kosovo Diplomatic Mission?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At that time there were two voices. One small still voice was ours and it said that we did not wish to conduct ethnic cleansing, that we wanted to punish all of our own criminals if they committed any crimes, that we wanted to engage in a political dialogue with the representatives of the Kosovo Albanians. However, our voice was not heard because the international media was saying that there were plans to perpetrate ethnic cleansing and drive out the Albanians. In order to defend ourselves from these false accusations in a desire to demonstrate that we are not a criminal government and we are not criminals, we sought internationally acceptable channels for the international public not to be informed on the events on Kosovo through journalists' reports on the BBC or the CNN, but to have qualified people arrive on the spot and confirm with their authority that our security forces were not engaged in organised and systematic crimes. We do not deny that, unfortunately, individual crimes and atrocities did happen, but what characterised our policy --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt but I think he's gone way beyond answering the question at this point in time. Did not several hundred foreign OSCE diplomats arrive? Yes or no would have been enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can put an additional question and you will get the same answer. I don't think he should be interrupted, but we can solve this right away. How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't -- you have an answer already which is wide-ranging. It is relevant, although it's not an answer to the question. If you want to pursue the matter in relation to other aspects, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please explain to the Court why we wanted an international mission, why we wanted foreign observers in Kosovo, because you just said that the federal government had exercised its powers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is that question not been answered, that it was to respond to false allegations by having independent people observe the activities of the forces? Is there something else you want from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness was interrupted. I think he should be allowed to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's sometimes difficult to answer directly. It's not a consequence of this agreement that several thousand monitors came. It's always just a first step. In order to get the monitors to come to an area, you have to deal with a number of issues such as the agreement with the OSCE mission. You have to know who's coming, you have to know what their numbers are, we have to guarantee the security of those people, we have to set up ways of communicating with them. This is an enormous task. It is precisely for that reason that I find it impossible to answer this question with a simple yes or no. In politics there is such a thing called a declaration. There is no doubt about it as far as this statement is concerned but implementation is a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What sort of decisions do you take as a federal government in terms of strengthening the presence of the federal government in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That was our basic approach. We were deeply convinced that the accusations being levelled against us for our policies in Kosovo and Metohija were inaccurate. We did everything in our power to prove our point. We opened Kosovo and Metohija to the presence of foreign diplomats. They started arriving in great numbers. In order to be able to communicate with them effectively, we simply moved a large number of our facilities and potential over to Kosovo and placed this at their disposal. They refused to go to Belgrade and sit there in our offices. They wanted to tour the area and see for themselves what the situation in Kosovo and Metohija really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. You in essence were prime minister. Did you take a decision to send anyone down there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you mean specifically, we took a decision to send a qualified mission there, many diplomats, assistants, people who were good at communicating. I decided they should be headed by the person normally in charge of foreign affairs in Yugoslavia, Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did they establish anything in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When we say the federal government, we must know that this comprised 12.000 clerks, clerical staff and administrators, who worked in numerous sections of the ministry. When I say "government," I mean the procedure. There were tons of documents being produced throughout this process. You can't just simply have a knee-jerk reaction and say, Okay, let's have a hundred monitors over there or over here. You have to make sure they have means of transportation, you have to make sure that they are safe. You have to do a whole number of serious things and the whole thing takes time. From the moment you sign an agreement to set up a mission, nobody should be naive enough to think the monitors can be dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija the next day. This takes time. It is a very responsible task and it is an enormous task. Thousands of professionals were involved. As for the political and diplomatic coordination at the time on behalf of the federal government, this was done by deputy prime minister. I decided that this should be so and this was perfectly in keeping with the procedures and the rules governing the work of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs set up its own HQ in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was indispensable. I'm grateful to all those people who did the job under very difficult circumstances on behalf of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You answered my next question in part. I'll try to cut it short. What about Mr. Sainovic, was he involved in foreign affairs in Mr. Kontic's previous government?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that there was a certain continuity and his new involvement was a direct consequence of that continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was involved in implementing the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Dayton Accords brought peace to the area, fortunately, and made possible a whole new approach, an approach of cooperation between parties that until not such a long time ago had been on the verge of conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you've long since answered that question. Please deal with each individual question rather than giving us a wide-ranging account of events or we'll never make progress here. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The authorisation that you granted Nikola Sainovic to deal with these issues, and we've specified what exactly already, was that based on the rules governing the work of the federal government? What was that based on? What would be the powers or the authority of a deputy prime minister? How do you appoint a deputy prime minister? How do you tell him to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There was a chancellor-based government and there were no restrictions on whoever was in office to appoint the cabinet. However, the government worked in line with its own internal regulations and based on a book of rules defining exactly what the prime minister was allowed to do and what the deputy prime minister was allowed to do and envisioning all the bodies and all the committees that they were to sit on in order to discuss government proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you take this decision to send Sainovic down to Kosovo and Metohija in terms of time, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in mid-June 1998, having observed for some time the political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us this briefly, please, what exactly was Sainovic doing in Kosovo and Metohija? We're looking at June, the summer of 1998, after you had sent him there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We had certain contacts. We had communication during our cooperation, and it was my understanding that while he was in Kosovo and Metohija he advocated the same political positions and pursued the same diplomatic activities that we as the federal government were pursuing, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he trying to secure the logistics support for all the foreign diplomats and everybody from the foreign agencies present in the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Given the circumstances and the conditions under which those people worked, it was necessary to do a lot of work under unstable circumstances with limited resources at our disposal. I suppose it was entirely necessary for them to communicate with each other in order to achieve the best results within the possibility that they had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the representatives of our bodies in Kosovo and Metohija? Did they have the know-how? Did they have the level of skill and the authorisation to communicate with someone that high-ranking?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They may have thought of themselves that way, but objectively speaking, it was necessary for high-ranking politicians, leaders, and professionals to come from the federal government. What I mean is all -- some of the ambassadors and our foreign ministry was full of ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Sainovic informing you about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and about his own involvement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We communicated officially at cabinet sessions. We were taking decisions, decisions that were based on a political insight into what exactly was going on. It wasn't just about Kosovo and Metohija, it was about the prevalent mood in the international community and they were following the whole thing closely. He gave a very significant contribution to the decision-making and, generally, the work of the federal cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, he was informing you about everything you needed to know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me now move on to something else. What steps did the state take to combat terrorist activity in Kosovo and Metohija, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more specific, please. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were saying that at the federal level no security was guaranteed and then you explained in relation to the Army of Yugoslavia the federal government was only in charge of the budget and the logistics and it had no powers at all over the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the federal Ministry of the Interior only protected foreign representatives which is an important task. So everything you've enumerated, is that all that the federal government could have done in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the federal government wanted to do something else, too, it wanted to create a political framework for an overall solution to the problem. I've stated this already. I do not wish to repeat myself. Everybody in their right state of mind knows that you cannot deal with a political problem by using weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know that an anti-terrorist operation took place which we believe was completed successfully sometime in October 1998 or September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who took those decisions? Where were the decisions made? Please bear in mind the Supreme Defence Council, the president, the MUP, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The main strategic decisions were adopted by the Supreme Defence Council. The implementation of those decisions was envisaged in great detail in the existing Laws on Defence and the Army of Yugoslavia. If, for example, the Supreme Defence Council says, We must defend our country, we must stifle terrorist activity, then that is decision enough. As far as I know about these things - and I've looked into it - you get the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army where the powers and duties of certain units are precisely defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will look into the Supreme Defence Council later on, but now I'm asking you about 1998. What I want to know is this: Who had the power to take the decision to use the MUP, the M-U-P, of Serbia, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The government alone, the minister of the interior of Serbia, but that decision too must be consistent with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean the Government of Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Given your high-ranking position at the time, do you believe that there existed a constitutional and legal basis to use the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia and Montenegro to combat terrorism in Kosovo in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, the basis existed. The federal government must determine the depth of the so-called border belt. It bases its decision on the constitution. It receives a proposal from the General Staff and determines how far the army can go in exercising its own duty, its own job. In 1987, when there was a crisis in Albania in 1997 [as interpreted], the Greek government broadened his border belt with Albania to 80 kilometres which means that at a range of 70 kilometres members of the border units were entitled to ID and send back people coming in from Albania. The federal government that I was heading at the time never declared this border belt to be broader than or deeper than 5 kilometres. It was because of the lie of the land. We needed to give sufficient room to the border units to protect both the border and themselves. There are some inaccessible areas in Kosovo and Metohija and Albania and what happened quite a number of times by 1987 and 1988 in those areas was that groups of armed people with pack animals reached at certain times certain points that we were unable to protect with more than four or five persons at the time. It's due to the lie of the land that it was impossible to do anything else to increase their presence. If you have 30 smugglers crossing a point like that, then you risk serious casualties among your own border officers. The government of Yugoslavia decided to increase, to broaden the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know if the Army of Yugoslavia could have been used to combat terrorism, to secure roads, to secure members of the Army of Yugoslavia, without necessarily introducing any of the so-called irregular states?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We spoke about that at the Supreme Defence Council in October and November 1998. I'm telling you about what I know. I'm telling you about my direct knowledge. The army was being used in compliance with orders from the federal government down the border belt, and then the army is used to defend itself and no order is required for something like that and you don't need to declare a state of war or anything like that. If someone fires at a soldier from a border unit, of course the soldier has no choice but to fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are two things that I wish to clarify. You seem to be suggesting that the Army of Yugoslavia acts in compliance with any orders from the federal government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't keep track. I'm trying to keep track but I can't but this is not something that I wanted to say. The Army of Yugoslavia needs a border belt. This border belt is set or determined by the government and it must have a constitution and legal basis for its functions in the defence of the country and the same thing applies to any country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as the summer of 1998 is concerned, was the Army of Yugoslavia used in compliance with the constitution and the law?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It is my deepest conviction that it was. I think everything that was done was perfectly in keeping with the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know how the anti-terrorist operation in 1998 was completed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. The conclusion was that the operation was successful, that the roads had now been cleared, the channels had now been re-opened. There were no major terrorist groups still active and this was the right time to start implementing a political solution, a political programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know how it was completed or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's my mistake. I'm probably talking too fast. I do know, I do know. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A little later was there an agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've mentioned that agreement already. Off the top of my head it was reached on the 13th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something entirely different now. You were in charge of the policies of the federal government. Let me ask you something about the policies of the federal government in Kosovo. How could you briefly define the policies pursued by the federal government in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998? I'm asking you just about that one year.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There was an offer of political dialogue that was meant to secure equal rights for all the ethnic groups in Kosovo and Metohija without necessarily jeopardizing the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Maybe my question wasn't as clear as it was meant to be. What did you do, what did you do within the government? Did you deal with that issue at your meetings? That was the sort of thing I was after.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Among other things, we would address the parliament, we addressed the public in its entirety. As a result of all these activities, a Federal Assembly was held on the 5th of October, 1998. I opened the meeting on behalf of the federal government and I put forward a set of political and other solutions in relation to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you to look at tab 2, Defence Exhibit 2D67. As you can see, this is a document that has several pages. We still know how to read, don't we, so don't read it out for us but just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to confirm that this document is a copy of the conclusions adopted by the Federal Assembly. I made an opening statement on behalf of the federal government at that session, and it gave me personal pleasure to see these conclusions adopted unanimously. This is a political programme, on the basis of which we and the government believed that it was possible to stabilise the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. There are several conclusions, political proposals, and assessments here but it shows a clear wish to state a clear position and to send a clear message to the Kosovo Albanians and the entire international community how the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia thinks that a solution should be found to stabilise the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be also -- it would also be helpful if you looked at paragraph 2 of this document and could you explain it in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean number 2 as such or do you mean the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 2 what is stated is yet another confirmation of principles among which dialogue is the first one. It shows that we don't think that the problem of violence can be resolved through the escalation of violence, but rather reverting to political dialogue. The next thing is respect for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and also equal rights of all citizens, all ethnic groups. This is a document that, unfortunately, did not become operative but I read it today with pride and pleasure because nothing can be found in it that would be against the civilisational principles of the era in which we live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, can you tell me what is meant by the equality of all citizens and all ethnic communities and groups in Kosovo without the possibility of anyone's predominance. What does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our political jargon, for years there had been a dilemma. The Albanians did not want to accept that they were a minority in Serbia, and they did accept that they were a majority in Kosovo. So there was this vicious circle of minority rights or anyone's domination. There is no doubt that the Albanians are majority in Kosovo and Metohija, but also it is undoubted that they are a minority as for all of the Republic of Serbia. So a solution cannot be found along those lines. Of course, equality of rights without predominance showed a readiness to discuss all these issues through dialogue and without resorting to arms and violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's all very well to talk in these broad terms of principle, but how do you actually achieve what you describe there as the equality of all citizens and all ethnic communities and groups? Does that mean it's not one man/one vote, but you have some other arrangement that will be a different form of democratic government or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honour, principles can only be discussed in general terms. If you go into implementation, then it's no longer principles, then it is imposing a particular model. This is an offer for dialogue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise for interfering. Do you, sir, also mean nobody will have a predominance, that means sort of equality in treatment, in matter of services, in matters -- other such matters, I mean, avoiding discrimination of any sort, do you mean to say that by what you have said in the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. I don't know how it can be put in simpler terms than we've put it here in this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I be of assistance. When you're talking about principles of equality among the communities, are you trying to say irrespective of size all communities are equal, regardless of whether there's a million of them or a hundred?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Equality of rights is absolute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see -- now hold on. Please don't put words into the witness's mouth. There is a very, very important difference between equality of citizens and equality of ethnic groups, a very clear difference, and that's what I'm trying to understand. We all know that this principle covers - as has been confirmed - equal treatment of citizens, but that -- this goes further, it goes into equality of groups which is a concept I have difficulty with in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
