utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I'd like to ask you to explain in more detail what this equality of communities means, in view of out-voting and all the other experience we had in the SFRY --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have given me a task that is very difficult. We lived for a long time in a communist system that spoke of the equality of rights of all nations and nationalities. Then after that we started building a democracy, where it was said that all people were equal and that they had the individual right, along with the collective dimension, to be different. That is the Serbian version of the English original. The individual right with a collective dimension shows precisely this. All ethnic communities and ethnic groups, irrespective of their size, enjoy equal rights according to the model that exists elsewhere in the world. We cannot say that Serbs and Albanians are the most equal in Kosovo because they constitute 90 per cent of the population. However, as far as I know, in the provisional government there were representatives of all the national and ethnic groups living in Kosovo, including the Turkish ethnic community that had 40.000 people and the Gorani and the Roma and the Catholic Albanians and the Muslims, who had specific characteristics of their own. However, building that kind of a model is terribly difficult, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In this same document you have Article 3. Could you tell us how the Federal Assembly assessed the root causes. That is under 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: May I repeat, all MPs supported this, all the conclusions were adopted unanimously. And it was stated the basic problem in Kosovo and Metohija is Albanian separatism, whose objective it is to dismember the Republic of Serbia and to cause a break-up of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So it's not equality of rights of Albanians or anybody else, but it is the assessment of all the political parties that were there, including the minority parties from Vojvodina, Sandzak, et cetera, that the central problem in Kosovo and Metohija is Albanian separatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. The next thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Who on that occasion represented Kosovo in the Assembly? Who was present on behalf of the constituencies of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there was no one because from as far back as 1991 [Realtime transcript read in error "1999"] they had left this project, taking part in this work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: However, that does not jeopardize the credibility and legitimacy of the Federal Assembly that was a significant and respected factor in international relations and all norms of international law were applied in respect of this Assembly. You know that anywhere else when someone decides to walk out, he cannot block cooperation as such. Our Assembly could not stop working just by virtue of the fact that Albanian representatives did not want to send their representatives to the Assembly of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the transcript there is a mistake. What is typed out is 1999. It's supposed to say 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when they had elections for the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when you said that there weren't any representatives from Kosovo, you were only referring to the Albanian majority parties, right, there were others?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already said. These people took part in the work of the provincial Executive Council and in the work of political parties, but objectively, they represented the minority of Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 4 now, paragraph 4 of this document and tell me what was the position of the Federal Assembly on the participation of the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP in these developments?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is put so concisely, I cannot put it in any better way than the way it is put here. The Federal Assembly gave full recognition to members of the Yugoslav Army and the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia who professionally, devotedly and with much courage and sacrifice protected our state border, smashed terrorist strongholds, prevented attempts at ethnic-cleansing by Albanian terrorists, and protected the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija from further suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you comment on paragraph 11, paragraph 11 of this same document. So what was the position of our state vis-a-vis the verification mission in Kosovo, in a sentence only.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Assembly supported the position of the federal government which means, in other words, that it was the federal government that proposed to the Federal Assembly that on the basis of the Moscow declaration by Presidents Yeltsin and Milosevic that we formally invite a mission of the OSCE to see for themselves positive developments in terms of the most important processes in Kosovo and Metohija. This is yet another manifestation of the openness of our country and its interest and readiness for equitable international cooperation. And another thing, briefly, time-frame work is very important. This is the 5th of October. On the basis of this open offer, Richard Holbrooke comes as a negotiator who then created the broadest possible international support: First, the Russian Federation, then the Federal Assembly, then the position of America to go for an agreement with the OSCE. Even according to literature, this is a procedure that you have to carry out as an equal and serious participant in international affairs and member of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Could you please look at 2D48, tab 3. Please also look at 2D57 under number 4. Could you give us your comments as to how the federal government treated citizens during this anti-terrorist action as can be seen in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my own experience, I confirmed that these are original documents from that period and they reflect the activity of the federal government at the time. Quick intervention was needed. People had to leave their homes, their homes were destroyed. They were internally displaced persons. You had to help them. In spite of the constant appeals that we were sending from the level of the federal government for people to remain at their homes, we knew that that could only be done if you gave them some kind of financial support. These documents only illustrate how the technology of decision-making took place within the federal government. We had to give them humanitarian assistance that was free of charge and that went to all, most of it to the Albanians by virtue of the fact that they constitute a vast majority of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is tab 4 just simply the covering note rather than the order itself of the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what the role of the federal government was in overcoming the crisis that you've already described that was caused by threats and blackmail coming from the international community in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, we were convinced that these assessments that were made about us were inaccurate and that they did not reflect -- and that they did not reflect reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In October 1998. It is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we're talking about the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were convinced that the positions that were predominant at that time among the public and in diplomatic consultations with us were wrong and that they did not correspond to the truth and that is why we decided to embark on the verification process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are the threats and blackmail you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I already spoke about that. That is to say that in the -- all of the world press was writing about NATO aggression that would be carried out against us. The newspaper Milliyet in Turkey, in October there were NATO carriers -- may I please just say this - that's on the front page. And then there is an interview with me stating, If you attack us, we will defend ourselves. Can there be a greater threat than that, having NATO threaten you as early as early October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's NATO you're referring to? You see the question was about threats and blackmail coming from the international community, so you're talking about blackmail by NATO, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about what was said in public and that cannot be challenged. In diplomatic contacts and in tete-a-tete contacts we were in a position to hear threats, blackmails, and all the rest, but I cannot prove that to you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Blackmail presupposes that you're told, Unless you do something, we will do something to you. So what is it the international community was demanding of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're coming to the period of the NATO air-strikes now or Rambouillet, where they said, Either agree to the occupation of part of your territory or leave your entire territory or we will bomb you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that the position in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was trying to say, Your Honour, that it was not only I who knew that. I could have imagined it. Kostas Simitis, the president -- the prime minister of Greece; the prime minister of Turkey; the prime minister of Macedonia, Crvenkovski; the prime minister of Bulgaria, Kostov, they all knew about it. They're all realistic politicians. You can't plan an attack on a country in a day or two, it's something that has to be planned for months and it's very difficult when you face the fact when everybody around you says you are going to be bombed but there is nothing we can do about it and we ourselves cannot do anything about it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The names of the prime ministers are not in the transcript. Can you repeat them, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The prime minister of Turkey was Mesut Yilmaz. The prime minister of Bulgaria was Kostov, Crvenkovski of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C-r-v-e-n-k-o-v-s-k-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did a situation then arise where Zivorad [as interpreted] Jovanovic the minister of foreign affairs concluded an agreement with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That was a diplomatic technological finale of what we were just discussing. Yeltsin, Holbrooke, and then finally Zivadin Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Up to the point in time when that was signed, did you have meetings or consultations in the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was such a huge task that many civil servants didn't have time to go home at all. Because to draw up such a large-scale agreement with so many precise principles, taking on this huge responsibility is not an easy task for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, the FRY, in spite of everything you've said about the NATO threats, did they conclude an agreement with him about the verification mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think on behalf of the army it was signed by General Perisic and that was one of those technical special agreements you had to have for modern technology to function, and you have to do that right away. You have to agree that a surveillance aircraft can -- can overlook and take photos without any hindrance anywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you now tell us what the standpoint of the FRY and the Republic of Serbia was towards the OSCE mission in general?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we wanted the mission to come. We invested a lot of effort in getting it there as soon as possible, and the most difficult part of the job was done in an admirably short period of time. However, days and weeks went by while the Kosovo Verification Mission was growing because it seemed to take a long time for them to decide who would be going to Kosovo. It took them much longer to do that than it took us to secure the conditions for their arrival in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how did the federal government cooperate with the OSCE to make all this operational? Did you have working bodies?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a task to which we gave high priority, and in accordance with our rules of procedure and our procedures in general, we set up a representation to cooperate with the OSCE. These were prominent members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in that mission, just give us their positions, their titles?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The mission or the commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The commission.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would help me if you were to give me a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But through reading Winston Churchill, I learned that you can set up a commission with the aim of not solving a problem or you can set one up with a wish to solve it. This one was set up in a desire to solve the problem. These were people of the highest professional integrity and we had the greatest confidence in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We'll come to that later on. Now let's look at the basis on which the commission was set up. Look at 2D346, that's tab 6. These are the rules of procedure of the federal government. Please look at Article 42. As we can all read my question is the following: Is this the basis pursuant to which the government was able to set up a provisional working body or committee?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the formal basis. I think it's the practice of all well-ordered bureaucratic structures or administrations to proceed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. We will now look at how working bodies of the government functioned in general. Look at Articles 33 and 34 of these rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Both 33 and 34, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does it follow? What does -- what follows from this? Why are working bodies set up?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for decades it was the practice in Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro to have cabinet sessions on a Thursday. That was the day when decisions would be issued. On every Tuesday, the working bodies and various commissions would meet so that everybody could build their administrative capacities into the making of a decision. It was only the government that could issue a decision, and it would enter into force once it was published in the Official Gazette and when it was signed by the prime minister. In order for the entire decision-making process to be a rational one, all the working bodies including all their members, would give proposals to the government. And in order to draw up these proposals, they would have a majority vote process. This was a highly complex bureaucratic mechanism which may not be the most efficient one but all the high-ranking state officials and civil servants and there were 12.000 of these had to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So they could not issue decisions but only make proposals to the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the cabinet could not enact a law, it could only table a bill in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, and the federal government would decide --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: By a majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember at whose proposal the commission for -- the federal commission for cooperation with the OSCE was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that came from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs because diplomats with long years of experience knew that this was the best way and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs spoke to Mr. Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what about the president of this commission, who nominated him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It was the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at 2D81, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This document, is that the basis of what we have just been talking about? Don't read it out just tell us what the most important points are.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is a cover letter sent with the agreement explaining the administrative procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it indicates that a number of federal ministries are involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that the procedure of adoption is quite an ambitious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And does it say here that the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs nominates Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the first passage on page 2 and it's signed by the Deputy Federal Minister Zoran Novakovic, a gentleman from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. And did the cabinet take a vote on this proposal and was it accepted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, look at 2D8, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, here you will find who the members were.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that this is a faithful copy. This is my signature, and to my recollection this is precisely the decision adopted by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you can see who the members were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What matters is that Nikola Sainovic was the president of the commission and I wish to mention for the sake of Their Honours that these people mentioned here were the most responsible people in their spheres of activity. And this shows that there was sincere wish to fulfil all the obligations undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now look at 2D9, please, tab 9. The document is 2D9 and this is a decision amending the previous or supplementing the previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again this is a document I signed, it's a valid document, and here more people who might be useful were appointed, who might be useful in the faster implementation of the tasks facing the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Now please look at tab 10, document 2D261. This is a proposal for -- of the decision to establish a federal commission of the federal government. Could you explain it a little bit? It's a draft decision. Is it in compliance with the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is, in fact, the same procedure done by the government but in the meantime, the circumstances have changed so this is a decision to form a federal government committee for cooperation with the UN mission which was already in Kosovo and Metohija [indiscernible] Resolution 1244. The names are different but the government commitment and the procedure adopted is the same as that adopted before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can one say that this was done in the same way, on the same legal basis as the commission for cooperation with the OSCE mission from October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's completely the same. I really believe that both before and after this the government used the same constitutional and legal framework. These are not two exceptions. These documents represent the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the date of the one we're now looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's after Resolution 1244 when UN troops entered instead of NATO. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who on our side gave the interpretation of the provisions of this agreement should there be any disagreements?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs because there were people there who knew all about the diplomatic presidents and the interpretations from previous periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at 2D179, tab 11. This is a report of the committee for foreign relations. Who was at the head of this committee?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Nikola Sainovic. This shows the methods by which the government communicated with international organisations. As members of the committee for the abolishing of racial discrimination, we were duty-bound to submit regular periodic reports, and this was done in a manner compliant with the rules of procedure of the federal government. This document shows that the entire legal procedure was respected in communication between the government and the relevant international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner we see that it's dated Belgrade 13th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have exhausted a part of my examination, and tomorrow I would like to embark on the part that deals with Rambouillet. So I think now might be a convenient moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Just one matter before we break. We have been trying to wrestle with the appropriate determination to make about expert reports for which there is at present no English version. In our communication with CLSS, we have tried to locate these reports. They have been unable to locate three of them, that's the reports by Stankovic, Jokic, and Simonovic. To enable them to do so, they need the job numbers, and you -- there was a communication sent to counsel asking for these, and no response. Now, are counsel in a position to give us these job numbers? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the CLSS system only allows one team member to have access to it and the registry will not pay for that person to be here; he's presently in the field. We did communicate the message to him yesterday. He's the only one that can get that specific number for us from the CLSS log-in. So we hope to have it by tomorrow, I'd imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He can do that remotely, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is an urgent matter, this. Because although the experts may not give evidence for some time, there may be issues that they are dealing with that are touched upon by other witnesses. So it's important that all this material should be available. So if there's any difficulty tomorrow, please advise us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will and I'm speaking as to the two that I'm aware of because we submitted two of the reports that you mentioned for translation. The third, I believe, was submitted by 1D -- the first Defence. So I'm speaking with respect to the Simonovic and the Stankovic reports which my team submitted for translation. I will have those numbers by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We'll check on it this evening as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Bulatovic, that completes our business for today. We will continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Overnight, and if you have to return yet again, it's vital that you have no communication with anyone about the evidence in the case. You're not barred from talking to people about things in general, but, please, in your discussions make no reference and listen to no words about the evidence either that you've given or that you are likely to give in the case. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher and return here at 9.00 tomorrow. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
